**Name (H1)**: Quantum Vault  — _read from web-demo/index.html_

**Subtitle**: 2-of-3 Shamir · AES-256-GCM · SMAUG-T · HAETAE  — _read from web-demo/index.html_

**Description**: Seals a secret under an AES-256-GCM key that is split 2-of-3 with Shamir, wraps each share with the SMAUG-T post-quantum KEM, and signs the container with HAETAE — so you can watch several primitives compose into one seal/open pipeline.  — _read from web-demo/index.html_

**Why it matters**: No single keyholder can open the vault and no lost key locks it forever — trust is spread across people, not staked on one. And because the wrapping is post-quantum, secrets sealed today should stay shut even after quantum computers arrive — provided the module-lattice problems underneath (MLWE/MLWR for SMAUG-T, MSIS for HAETAE) stay hard against quantum algorithms. Believed, not proven.  — _read from web-demo/index.html_

**Card copy**: Threshold short-secret encryption using secret sharing and Korean post-quantum cryptography, compiled to WASM for direct browser use.

**Chips**: AES-256-GCM · Shamir SSS · SMAUG-T · HAETAE

**Implements**: AES `web-demo/src/crypto/aes.ts:9`, AES-GCM `web-demo/src/crypto/aes.ts:10`, HAETAE `wasm/src/haetae_exports.c:2`, HKDF `crates/qv-core/src/encrypt.rs:20`, PBKDF2 `web-demo/src/crypto/keywrap.ts:49`, SHA-256 `web-demo/src/crypto/keywrap.ts:49`, Shamir secret sharing `web-demo/src/crypto/pipeline.ts:16`, SMAUG-T `wasm/src/smaug_exports.c:2`

**Standards body**: IETF, NIST

**Stated limitations (page)**:

- _(disclaimer, web-demo/index.html)_ ⚠️ Disclaimers Educational only — do not use for production data protection. No independent production attestation — competition analysis and this repository review are not a formal audit of the deployed composition. Browser WASM has not been established as constant-time. Side-channel resistance is not guaranteed.

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Too few shares means permanent loss.** Shamir reconstruction needs at least the threshold number of valid shares; lose more than `n − t` and the secret is gone for good, with no fallback because nothing else holds the key.
- **AES-GCM nonce reuse is catastrophic.** Reusing a (key, nonce) pair under AES-256-GCM leaks relationships between plaintexts and enables practical forgeries, breaking both confidentiality and integrity.
- **Plain Shamir does not detect bad shares.** Basic secret sharing has no built-in cheater detection, so a corrupted or maliciously altered share can silently produce a wrong reconstruction unless a verifiable scheme is layered on top.
- **Threshold choice is a security/availability tradeoff.** A low threshold makes recovery easy but also makes compromise easy (fewer shares to steal); a high threshold resists compromise but raises the risk of being unable to reassemble enough shares.
- **KpqC competition selection is not publication as a standard.** SMAUG-T and HAETAE are final KpqC competition algorithms, but the [April 2026 status notice](https://kpqc.or.kr/contents/03_exhibit/board.html?board_id=board_competition&mode=view&no=12) says SMAUG-T was proposed for Korean-standard development while HAETAE remained under review. Neither selection alone is a published Korean Standard, and parameters or encodings can still change during standardization.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 10348 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is
Quantum Vault is a browser demo that combines AES-256-GCM, Shamir SSS / GF(2⁸), SMAUG-T (스마우그-T) KEM, and HAETAE (해태) signature in one sealing/opening pipeline. It is built to show how a secret can be encrypted once, split into threshold shares, and opened only when enough valid shares are recovered. SMAUG-T handles post-quantum key encapsulation for per-share wrapping, and HAETAE checks the signature under the container’s included, unpinned key before decryption; that does not authenticate the original sender. The security model is hybrid: symmetric encryption plus post-quantum asymmetric primitives with threshold reconstruction. A plain-language **"How this box works"** walkthrough tells the four-primitive envelope story in order, per-step narration lights up as each pipeline stage runs, and a Shamir key-strip visualization shows the real 32-byte AES key splitting into 3 shares and re-forming from any 2 (or producing an unauthenticated candidate from just 1). On open, real recovered share strips combine into the reconstructed key. There is no independent original-key reference or per-byte comparison: copying the reconstruction would not supply evidence. The strip is confirmed only by successful AES-GCM authenticated decryption; two recovered shares alone cannot establish successful opening. Failed authentication leaves it unconfirmed, and one share is below threshold. An "inside step 3" mini-diagram separates the password-protected secret-key path from KEM encapsulation/decapsulation and explains that defeating either route can expose a share; their strengths are not additive. A small 2-D lattice sketch introduces the assumptions motivating the post-quantum design without presenting them as proof. Inline glossary tooltips introduce KEM, Shamir/GF(2⁸), "lattice-based", and sign-vs-verify for newcomers; a classical-vs-post-quantum toggle and a one-click tamper demo make the "harvest now, decrypt later" motivation and the confidentiality-vs-integrity failure distinction concrete; expert-facing "when to use each primitive" reference cards are gated behind a **Go deeper** reveal so the first-scroll path stays focused on the interactive core.
```

**Name (H1)**: Key Lifecycle  — _read from index.html_

**Subtitle**: NIST SP 800-57 · Rotation · Compromise  — _read from index.html_

**Description**: Encrypt fictional records, copy an old key, rotate, and verify why captured ciphertext remains exposed.  — _read from index.html_

**Why it matters**: Rotating a key protects new records, but it cannot erase a stolen historical key or an attacker’s copy of old ciphertext. An authentic AES-GCM decrypt can still reveal data after a compromise.  — _read from index.html_

**Card copy**: Follow ten key-management decisions, then rotate real AES-GCM keys and test why a copied old key still decrypts an attacker’s archived ciphertext.

**Name (H1)**: Compression Leak  — _read from index.html_

**Subtitle**: BREACH · gzip · AES-GCM  — _read from index.html_

**Description**: Compress and encrypt synthetic responses and discover what ciphertext length reveals.  — _read from index.html_

**Why it matters**: Compressing private data together with attacker-controlled text can make the encrypted response length depend on secret matches. Authentication still succeeds: the leaked information comes from length, not broken AES.  — _read from index.html_

**Card copy**: Compress a secret beside an attacker-controlled guess, then encrypt with AES-GCM. Measure real ciphertext lengths and test why separating compression contexts changes the leak.

**Name (H1)**: Subliminal Channels  — _read from index.html_

**Subtitle**: ECDSA P-256 · RFC 6979  — _read from index.html_

**Description**: Sign the same document in different valid ways and read the additional symbol carried in a signature.  — _read from index.html_

**Name (H1)**: Phantom Vault  — _read from src/main.ts_

**Subtitle**: Stateless password derivation · PBKDF2 → HMAC-DRBG → rejection sampling  — _read from src/main.ts_

**Description**: Regenerate a site-specific password on demand from a master passphrase plus context, watching PBKDF2 key-stretch, HMAC-DRBG, and rejection sampling build it step by step — with nothing stored.  — _read from src/main.ts_

**Why it matters**: No stored vault means no vault database to breach or sync — the risk moves to your master passphrase and the device deriving from it. Bump the version to rotate a leaked password, and context keeps each site independent — but effective strength is capped by that passphrase.  — _read from src/main.ts_

**Card copy**: Derive any password from a master passphrase using HMAC-DRBG. Nothing stored, nothing synced, nothing left behind to breach.

**Chips**: PBKDF2-SHA-256 · HMAC-DRBG · Rejection Sampling

**Implements**: HMAC `src/crypto/hmac-drbg.ts:36`, HMAC-DRBG `src/crypto/hmac-drbg.ts:53`, PBKDF2 `src/crypto/pbkdf2.ts:32`, SHA-256 `src/crypto/hmac-drbg.ts:42`

**Attacks shown**: Brute force `src/main.ts:140`, Dictionary attack `README.md:32`

**References**: Argon2, CTR-DRBG, HKDF, SHA-1, bcrypt, scrypt

**Standards body**: IETF, NIST

**Implementation**: WebCrypto

**Spec citations, exactly as written**:

- `NIST SP 800-132` — first seen README.md:45 (3×)
- `NIST SP 800-90A` — first seen README.md:63 (1×)
- `NIST SP 800-90A Rev 1` — first seen src/crypto/hmac-drbg.ts:51 (3×)
- `NIST SP 800-90A Rev.1` — first seen README.md:46 (4×)
- `RFC 8018` — first seen README.md:44 (1×)
- `SP 800-90A Rev.1` — first seen README.md:5 (6×)

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- Master passphrase compromise cascades globally: if an attacker learns the passphrase, every derived credential can be regenerated.
- Weak or low-entropy passphrase selection: deterministic generation cannot compensate for guessable input material.
- Context collisions (`service`, `username`, `version`) across accounts: reused context produces identical outputs and defeats separation.
- Incorrect implementation of rejection sampling: modulo-biased mapping would skew distribution and reduce effective password strength.
- Operational misuse of versioning: failing to track version changes can lock users out after rotation.
```

```markdown
## What It Is

Phantom Vault is a stateless password derivation demo that combines PBKDF2-SHA-256, HMAC-DRBG (SP 800-90A Rev.1 §10.1.2), and rejection sampling to deterministically produce service-specific passwords. It solves the problem of storing synced password vault data by regenerating credentials from a master passphrase plus context (`service`, `username`, and `version`). The model is symmetric and deterministic: whoever knows the same inputs can regenerate the same output. This is not asymmetric cryptography, zero-knowledge proof storage, or threshold key management, and it does not provide account recovery if the passphrase is lost.
```

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- Trusting a generator because one sample passes statistical tests: the Dual_EC-style model can pass these four checks yet remain predictable to the trapdoor holder. This is not the full SP 800-22 battery or a certification of security.
- Adopting unverifiable "magic constants": when generator constants cannot be independently re-derived, a standards body or vendor can embed a trapdoor that users can never detect from the output alone.
- DRBG state compromise without reseeding: an attacker who recovers internal state can predict all future output until the generator is reseeded with fresh entropy.
- Insufficient entropy at seed time: a DRBG is only as strong as its seed, so low-entropy or predictable seeding makes the output guessable regardless of the algorithm.
- Output-truncation assumptions: Dual\_EC's relatively small truncation left enough bits in each block to make state recovery cheap for the trapdoor holder.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 10174 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

Corrupted Oracle compares **HMAC-DRBG** (NIST SP 800-90A §10.1.2) and **ChaCha20-DRBG** (RFC 8439-based) with a **simplified Dual_EC-style educational model**. The model uses real P-256 elliptic curve arithmetic and a live trapdoor attack inspired by the historical Dual_EC_DRBG construction. It is not an implementation of the complete January 2012 SP 800-90A §10.3.1 lifecycle. It shows why passing statistical tests does not establish unpredictability: knowledge of the secret relationship between P and Q can recover the model's internal state and predict subsequent output until reseeding.
```

Full README: https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-corrupted-oracle/blob/HEAD/README.md

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 4577 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

Air Stream is a browser lab for the three deployed 128-bit 3GPP confidentiality families: 128-EEA1 with SNOW 3G, 128-EEA2 with AES-CTR, and 128-EEA3 with ZUC. It computes each keystream from the same key, COUNT, bearer, direction, and length, then checks each family against published implementors' data. The demo isolates confidentiality generation and keystream reuse; it does not model cellular attachment, key derivation, or a complete NAS/AS protocol. It is not production crypto.
```

**Description**: Runs AIMer sign and verify plus NTRU+ encapsulate and decapsulate, completing the four-algorithm KpqC set alongside Quantum Vault.  — _read from index.html_

**Why it matters**: National post-quantum suites can cover the same jobs while making different hardness bets. Here, an NTRU-family lattice KEM sits beside a signature built from a symmetric one-way function and MPC-in-the-Head.  — _read from index.html_

**Card copy**: Historical AIM2-based AIMer signing, with a reported public-key-only forgery vulnerability (ePrint 2026/2235, September 28, 2026), beside NTRU+ from the older NTRU line. Honest round trips do not establish signature security.

**Stated limitations (page)**:

- _(honesty, src/ui/aimerPane.ts)_ Historical AIM2 — reported forgery vulnerability. ePrint 2026/2235 (September 28, 2026) reports public-key-only forgeries against AIMer v2.0 accepted by unmodified reference verifiers. This is a demonstrated result reported in a preprint; it has not yet been independently reproduced against this lab's shipped WASM. Honest KATs and one-bit tamper rejection do not establish signature security. AIM3-based v3.0 excludes this zero-branch attack, without a comprehensive security assessment here.
- _(caveat, src/ui/aimerPane.ts)_ Each cell is one repetition's real proof block, sliced at its true offset in this signature. Which party is hidden in a repetition is not decoded here — that index comes from the verifier's Fiat-Shamir expansion of h2, and the reference package ships WASM binaries with no source to confirm the expansion against. What is measured instead: flip a bit in any one block and the real verifier rejects.
- _(honesty, src/ui/aimerPane.ts)_ Accepted, not proven hard. The real verifier accepts this honest signature, but acceptance does not establish knowledge of a valid preimage in this historical relation. That success is not a proof that AIM2 is one-way. See the reported public-key-only forgery vulnerability above. The browser WASM is not guaranteed constant-time and is not production crypto.
- _(honesty, src/ui/ntruplusPane.ts)_ Research update — October 19, 2026. de Perthuis and Trenkić, How Secure are NTRU+ Keys? (ePrint 2026/2527) is a preprint received October 18 and published October 19. Its simulation-based estimates find the best module attack saves 4–10 BKZ block sizes, at most three bits in the Core-SVP cost model. The analyzed NTRU+ parameterizations remain safe within the authors' analysis.
- _(honesty, src/ui/ntruplusPane.ts)_ Matched, not proven hard. The sender and recipient agree here, but a round trip does not prove the NTRU problem is hard. This reference WASM is newer and less cross-implementation-scrutinized than the NIST FIPS selections, is not guaranteed constant-time, and is not production crypto.

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **A tampered signature or ciphertext that still verifies.** This is the alarm
  state for the specific one-bit edits exercised here, and the e2e suite fails if
  those edits paint an alarm verdict. This is not a universal forgery-rejection
  guarantee; see the reported AIMer relation flaw above.
- **Transcribing the AIM affine layer wrong.** The affine layer is the easy
  transcription error in AIM, and a wrong one still produces plausible-looking hex.
  It is caught because the computed image has to equal the reference's public-key
  image; perturbing the triangular masks, the matrix order, the SHAKE seed, the pi
  constants, the reduction polynomial or the feed-forward XOR each break that
  equality.
- **Reducing the NTRU+ ring with the wrong sign.** `X^768 = X^384 - 1` has a minus
  sign that is easy to lose; both reduction terms are mutation-tested.
- **Reading the MPCitH view as more than it is.** The reduced transcript view shows
  33 repetitions of a 16-party simulation. It does **not** decode which party is
  hidden per repetition, and it does not imply the full soundness of the parameter
  set — see below.
- **WASM failing to load.** Both panes degrade to an explicit failure verdict naming
  the error. They never fabricate a result.
```

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Large signatures** — the deterministic Shipovnik fixture is 805,868 bytes;
  its API reserves a 1,072,662-byte maximum. Correct verification does not make
  that bandwidth cost disappear.
- **Slow portable signing** — measured cold/warm Hypericum `m_128_20` WASM
  fixture runs took 11–83 seconds on the development machine. Signing runs in a
  worker and never substitutes a fake signature while waiting.
- **Hash assumptions remain hash assumptions** — Hypericum's green verifier
  does not provide security beyond its hash functions, parameters, and complete
  construction.
- **Endianness drift** — Streebog-256 and Streebog-512 byte order is pinned by
  GOST vectors, the QApp fixture digests, and cross-lab package consistency.
- **Reduced-model confusion** — the visible Merkle slice and one Stern round
  execute real operations but deliberately use small dimensions for inspection.
```

**Name (H1)**: SM2 Forge  — _read from src/ui/app.ts_

**Subtitle**: GB/T 32918 · GM/T 0003 · RFC 8998  — _read from src/ui/app.ts_

**Description**: Run real SM2 signatures and encryption, inspect the identity prefix, and decode both ciphertext byte orders.  — _read from src/ui/app.ts_

**Why it matters**: Adopting a national crypto suite is not a curve swap. SM2 signatures bind an identity, and two valid ciphertext serializations can still break interoperability.  — _read from src/ui/app.ts_

**Card copy**: Sign and encrypt under GB/T 32918 SM2, read the identity digest that precedes every signature, compare both deployed ciphertext orders, then recover a key from a reused nonce.

**Chips**: SM2 · SM3 · Nonce Reuse · RFC 8998

**Implements**: SM2 `src/sm2/sm2.ts:113`, SM3 `src/sm2/sm2.ts:1`

**Attacks shown**: Key recovery `README.md:5`, Nonce reuse `src/attack/nonce-reuse.ts:4`, Side-channel (unspecified) `README.md:51`

**References**: EC point arithmetic, ECDSA, P-256, P-384, Schnorr, TLS 1.3

**Standards body**: ISO

**Implementation**: @noble

**Spec citations, exactly as written**:

- `RFC 8998` — first seen README.md:3 (7×)

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Identity mismatch** — a signer and verifier that use different IDs compute different Z_A values and verification fails.
- **Serialization mismatch** — `C1C3C2` bytes fed to a `C1C2C3` decoder fail the SM3 integrity check even though both layouts are valid conventions.
- **Nonce reuse** — two signatures over different messages under one `k` expose `d`; the recovered scalar re-derives the victim public key exactly.
- **Malformed C1** — decryption rejects a point that is not on curveSM2 before deriving a shared point.
- **Invalid private key** — SM2 excludes `d = n - 1` because `(1 + d)` would not be invertible modulo `n`.
```

**Subtitle**: MISTY1 &middot; KASUMI &middot; Related-Key  — _read from index.html_

**Description**: Run MISTY1 and KASUMI side by side, inspect the parts changed for cellular hardware, and execute the seven-round distinguisher those changes enabled.  — _read from index.html_

**Why it matters**: A security argument belongs to one exact design, not to its name or round count. Simplifying a proven structure can silently remove the assumptions that made its bound hold.  — _read from index.html_

**Card copy**: Run MISTY1 and KASUMI side by side, map the design changes between them, and execute the seven-round related-key sandwich distinguisher in the page.

**Stated limitations (page)**:

- _(honesty, src/ui/attackPane.ts)_ ! KASUMI: broken in the related-key model — NOT a live GSM-call break.
- _(caveat, src/ui/diffPane.ts)_ No single edited box is "the bug." The attack uses an alignment of the linear key schedule, changed inner functions, and round placement. The MISTY1 proof covers the original whole design, not any eight-round descendant.

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Confusing equal dimensions with equal security** — both designs have eight rounds, 64-bit blocks, and 128-bit keys, but the MISTY1 bounds do not transfer to KASUMI.
- **Overclaiming the attack** — the full result uses four related keys and adaptive chosen data; a passive GSM listener does not receive that capability.
- **Mistaking the browser exhibit for full recovery** — this lab executes the seven-round distinguisher. It reports, but does not run, the full eight-round key-recovery work.
- **Using educational implementations operationally** — the code prioritizes transparency and is not constant-time or independently audited.
```

```markdown
**MISTY1 · KASUMI · Related-Key**

A browser-only lab that runs real MISTY1 and KASUMI side by side, maps the design changes between them, and executes the seven-round related-key sandwich distinguisher from Dunkelman, Keller, and Shamir.
```

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- An 80-bit input label does not provide 80-bit resistance when initialization compresses the key to 32 bits.
- A short known-keystream sample can create false positives, so the lab requires at least four bytes and verifies every recovered candidate byte-for-byte.
- An all-zero known-plaintext fixture can obscure what is plaintext, ciphertext, and keystream, so the UI rejects it.
- A browser cannot honestly claim to sweep all $2^{32}$ candidates interactively; the page labels its $2^{16}$ window and reports the exact number tested.
- A stale recovery is not evidence for changed inputs; changing the key, frame, or known plaintext retires the verdict.
- A rate measured once, in one browser, on one machine is not a cost model; Exhibit 5 labels every projected figure an extrapolation and refuses to render any of them until the learner's own run has produced a rate.
- A scale-up multiplier is an assumption, not a measurement, so Exhibit 5 makes all three editable, prints the one in force, and labels a multiplier past $10^{21}$ absurd instead of quietly computing it.
- A timer too coarse for a fast run makes a rate a lower bound, and a device below one candidate per second makes it a floor; both states say so rather than presenting a derived number as measured.
- "Broken" in a paper and "broken" on a radio are different events: the best published single-key attack on full AES is 2.49 bits faster than brute force, which is a result and not a threat.
- An attack model is part of the result, so every row names it; the related-key figures far below the brute-force line assume keys related by attacker-chosen differences, which a protocol does not hand out.
- Reduced-round cryptanalysis is a different measurement from full-round key recovery, so this lab plots only the latter and defers the round-count view to Iron Serpent.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 9357 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

Export Grade is a browser lab for the TEA1 air-interface stream cipher used by TETRA. It runs a TypeScript port of Midnight Blue's reverse-engineered TEA1, verifies it against the upstream known-answer tests, exposes the function that reduces a ten-byte key to one 32-bit register, and searches a labeled browser-sized part of that effective space. It then takes the rate that search measured on the learner's own machine and extrapolates it across larger keyspaces, and sets that cost beside the published cryptanalysis of full-round AES.

The cryptography and search are real. For tractability, the page selects the $2^{16}$ window containing its local fixture's register; it does not search all $2^{32}$ candidates. The page uses local fixtures rather than intercepted traffic. This is not production cryptography or an operational TETRA tool.
```

**Name (H1)**: DRBG Arena  — _read from src/main.ts_

**Subtitle**: HMAC · CTR · Hash_DRBG · NIST SP 800-90A  — _read from src/main.ts_

**Description**: Seed each of the three NIST-approved DRBGs and watch a high-entropy seed expand through the seed → state → output → reseed lifecycle into a deterministic pseudorandom stream.  — _read from src/main.ts_

**Why it matters**: Keys, nonces, and IVs are only as safe as the generator behind them. A DRBG must stay unpredictable even if its state leaks, and passing statistical tests proves nothing — Dual_EC looked random too.  — _read from src/main.ts_

**Card copy**: Explore HMAC_DRBG, CTR_DRBG, and Hash_DRBG state and reseeding. Compare statistical tests, including a signed monobit exercise, and distinguish plausible output from seed freshness and credited entropy.

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Insufficient entropy at seeding.** A DRBG is only as strong as its seed; seeding from a low-entropy or predictable source makes all output predictable regardless of the algorithm.
- **No reseeding or prediction resistance.** Generating indefinitely from one seed without reseeding means a future state compromise can expose subsequent output; SP 800-90A defines reseed limits for a reason.
- **State compromise and backtracking.** If the internal state leaks, an implementation without proper backtracking resistance can let an attacker reconstruct previously generated values.
- **Choosing a non-CSPRNG.** Using `Math.random()` or other statistical (non-cryptographic) generators for keys, nonces, or IVs defeats the entire scheme.
- **Trusting statistical tests for security.** A fixed or public seed can produce statistically plausible output. Repeating it reproduces the stream and its test scores; these tests do not establish seed freshness, secrecy, unpredictability, or absence of a backdoor. [NIST SP 800-22 Rev. 1a (2010)](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/22/r1/upd1/final) explicitly says statistical testing cannot replace cryptanalysis. Exhibit 5’s Dual_EC row remains an OS-randomness stand-in, not an implementation of Dual_EC.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 12942 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

DRBG Arena demonstrates the three NIST SP 800-90A approved Deterministic Random Bit Generators: HMAC_DRBG, CTR_DRBG, and Hash_DRBG. Each construction takes entropy from a true random source and produces a cryptographically secure pseudorandom output stream. This demo is the correct-case companion to [Corrupted Oracle](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-corrupted-oracle/), which shows what happens when a DRBG is intentionally backdoored (Dual_EC_DRBG). The security model is symmetric: all output is deterministically derived from the seed, computationally indistinguishable from true randomness, and resistant to backtracking and prediction attacks.
```

**Name (H1)**: BB84  — _read from index.html_

**Subtitle**: Quantum Key Distribution · Bennett–Brassard 1984  — _read from index.html_

**Description**: Simulate preparation, measurement and sifting, then compare sampled error rates with and without an intercept-resend Eve; full interception gives about 25% QBER on an ideal noiseless channel.  — _read from index.html_

**Why it matters**: Under a specified device model, an authenticated classical channel and appropriate post-processing, QKD can bound an eavesdropper's knowledge without computational hardness assumptions. A finite error sample does not guarantee detection of every eavesdropper.  — _read from index.html_

**Card copy**: A classical BB84 teaching simulation with basis sifting, QBER, and illustrative SHA-256 key derivation for AES-GCM. An optional reconciliation and Toeplitz extraction exercise shows public leakage and an assumed entropy budget; it does not prove finite-key QKD security.

**Chips**: Photon Polarization · Basis Sifting · QBER · SHA-256 Key Derivation

**Implements**: AES `src/encrypt.ts:37`, AES-GCM `src/encrypt.ts:37`, BB84 `src/bb84.ts:186`, SHA-256 `src/bb84.ts:175`, Toeplitz extractor `src/teaching.ts:76`

**Stated limitations (page)**:

- _(caveat, index.html)_ Starts at zero because this simulation cannot infer Eve's conditional knowledge from QBER. Enter a hypothetical bound between zero and the retained length. A zero-bit result is valid; extracted bits are not used as an AES-256 key here.

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Unauthenticated classical channel:** BB84 needs an authenticated public channel for basis reconciliation; without authentication an active attacker can mount a man-in-the-middle on the sifting step.
- **Channel noise vs. eavesdropping:** real QBER mixes natural noise with any eavesdropping, so the detection threshold trades false alarms against missed detection.
- **Hardware side channels:** real photon sources leak — multi-photon pulses enable photon-number-splitting attacks, and detector-blinding attacks have broken deployed QKD links.
- **Classical post-processing still matters:** error correction and privacy amplification must be done correctly, or the final key is not secret even when the QBER looks fine. The main run hashes unreconciled bits and has no finite-key privacy-amplification proof. The optional small-code exercise assumes its entropy bound instead of estimating one, and its extracted bits are never used for the AES message. Retained-bit disagreement in the main run can leave Alice and Bob with different AES keys.
- **Early basis announcement:** if the protocol lets an attacker delay quantum delivery until after Alice reveals her bases, a quantum-memory Eve in this model learns the sifted bits without inducing QBER. The optional timeline compares that flaw with receipt-first ordering; authentication and timing assumptions still matter.
- **This is a classical simulation:** it models the protocol with a CSPRNG, not real quantum states, so it cannot provide the physical security guarantees of true QKD hardware.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 10350 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

Browser-based simulation of the BB84 Quantum Key Distribution protocol (Bennett & Brassard, 1984). BB84 is the first quantum cryptography protocol, and one of a family of QKD key-exchange methods (E91, B92 and others followed) whose security proofs use quantum physics rather than computational hardness assumptions, under specified device and authenticated-channel models. The main demo simulates six steps classically: photon preparation, measurement, basis sifting, QBER error estimation, SHA-256 key derivation (an illustrative stand-in for privacy amplification), and AES-256-GCM encryption. Its full intercept-resend Eve produces about 25% QBER on an ideal noiseless channel; that number is not a universal eavesdropping signature.

The main run deliberately leaves out **information reconciliation** (error correction) and shows the result. Alice and Bob each derive their own key from their own bits, and step 6 encrypts under Alice's key and decrypts under Bob's — so whenever noise or an undetected Eve flipped a retained bit, the two keys differ and AES-GCM's tag check refuses the message. At the default 256 photons and 1% noise that happens in roughly half of runs (measured over 300 simulated runs); set noise to 0% and run without Eve and the keys agree every time. That failure is the lesson: sifting plus illustrative hashing alone does not give you a shared key over a real channel. The optional post-processing experiment below lets you explore an explicitly limited repair after the main run.
```

Full README: https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-bb84/blob/HEAD/README.md

**Name (H1)**: Shor's Algorithm  — _read from index.html_

**Subtitle**: Quantum period-finding · QFT · continued fractions  — _read from index.html_

**Description**: Factor an integer N by turning it into quantum order-finding: extract the period of a mod N via the QFT and continued fractions, then recover the factors with gcd(a^(r/2)±1, N).  — _read from index.html_

**Why it matters**: RSA, ECC, and Diffie-Hellman all rest on factoring and discrete logs being hard — the same problems Shor solves in polynomial time. A large enough quantum computer would break the encryption guarding nearly every website, bank, and message.  — _read from index.html_

**Card copy**: Modular period finding with QFT and continued fractions to recover integer factors, showing why RSA, ECC, and Diffie-Hellman must migrate to post-quantum alternatives.

**Chips**: Shor's Algorithm · Period Finding · QFT · RSA Factorization

**Implements**: Shor's algorithm `src/shor.ts:82`

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- Period finding fails when the random base `a` shares a factor with N, or when the recovered period `r` is odd or yields a^(r/2) ≡ -1 (mod N) — these cases produce only trivial factors and force a restart with a new base.
- The QFT measurement is probabilistic: a run can land on a peak that does not reveal the true period, so several runs may be needed.
- Continued-fraction convergents can return a divisor of the period rather than the period itself, which is why the a^r ≡ 1 (mod N) check is required before trusting a result.
- The simulation classically tracks the full state, so it only scales to small N (the demo caps at N < 10,000) — it is not a quantum computer.
- Misreading the threat scope: Shor breaks factoring and discrete log (RSA, ECC, classical DH) but not symmetric ciphers or hashes beyond Grover's quadratic speedup.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 9928 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

Shor's algorithm (Peter Shor, 1994) is a quantum algorithm that factors integers in polynomial time O((log N)³), rendering RSA, ECC, and all discrete-logarithm-based cryptosystems insecure against a sufficiently large quantum computer. This demo models the complete teaching pipeline — classical pre-checks, modular exponentiation period finding, a windowed Quantum Fourier Transform probability shape, continued fraction extraction, and GCD-based factor recovery — entirely in the browser with no backends. The QFT sampler covers all `r` peak neighbourhoods but keeps only offsets within ±4 and treats those neighbourhoods as equally likely; it is an explicitly bounded classical approximation, not a full-state quantum simulation. The security model it breaks is asymmetric public-key cryptography; it does not threaten symmetric ciphers or hash functions beyond Grover's quadratic speedup.

Beyond executing the steps, the demo is built to teach the two leaps that make Shor click: **why knowing the period `r` factors `N`** (an always-visible explainer walks `aʳ ≡ 1 → (a^(r/2)−1)(a^(r/2)+1) ≡ 0 → gcd(a^(r/2)±1, N)`, with the actual numbers from your run substituted in), and **why the QFT concentrates probability at multiples of `Q/r`** (animated *phasor wheels* draw the rotating phase of each comb entry so you can watch them constructively add at `k·Q/r` and cancel elsewhere — the real interference `|Σ eⁱᶲ|²`, not a pre-plotted curve). Every quantum step is labelled **(classically simulated)** so a browser demo can teach a quantum algorithm without ever implying real quantum speedup.
```

Full README: https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-shor/blob/HEAD/README.md

**Stated limitations (page)**:

- _(caveat, src/main.ts)_ Historical logical-circuit estimate (Grassl et al. 2016), not a wall-clock prediction. The headline “2^${iterExp}” counts iterations; the real work is iterations × cost-per-iteration. Depth counts sequential circuit layers; width counts logical qubits. Qubit-cycles measure space-time volume and require a width schedule. Physical error-correction overhead and wall-clock timing are not included. This construction estimate is not a universal lower bound. Resource accounting and later constructions.

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Reading the key-halving as literal feasibility** — "AES-128 → 2^64" is an idealized query count; the per-iteration oracle is a full AES circuit and Grover is inherently sequential, so the real cost is far higher and AES-128 is not practically broken by it.
- **Assuming Grover parallelizes the depth away** — it gives at most a quadratic speedup, and splitting it across machines splits the √N benefit; you cannot brute-force the circuit depth down the way classical search parallelizes.
- **Running too many iterations** — past k* = π/4·√N the state rotates past the target and success probability falls (overshoot); more iterations is not better.
- **Applying it to the wrong primitive** — Grover threatens symmetric keys and hash preimages, not RSA/ECC/DH (that is Shor). Conflating the two misstates the risk.
- **Treating O(√N) as beatable** — the BBBV bound proves no quantum search does better; assuming a future faster generic search is unfounded.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 10642 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

Grover's algorithm (Lov Grover, 1996) is a quantum search algorithm that finds a marked item in an unstructured search space of N items using O(√N) queries — a quadratic speedup over classical brute force. This demo classically simulates the complete amplitude amplification process with exact mathematical formulas: oracle phase kickback, inversion-about-mean diffusion, and probability oscillation including overshoot past optimal iterations. The security model is symmetric cryptography — Grover is the quantum threat to AES, SHA, and HMAC that Shor's algorithm does not touch. Grover's speedup is provably optimal (BBBV lower bound); no quantum algorithm can search faster than O(√N).
```

Full README: https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-grover/blob/HEAD/README.md

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **The threat model mismatch:** This attack requires both an encryption oracle
  AND a decryption oracle that accepts 2^128 forgery attempts. If your deployment
  cannot expose a decryption oracle to adversaries, that specific attack model
  does not apply; this alone does not prove HiAE’s 256-bit claim or settle other security goals.
- **Toy scale vs full scale:** The live recovery brute-forces a *disclosed
  toy keyspace of the learner's chosen width, up to 2^16,* against real oracle output (the differential-step panel is
  the paper's own technique, but at one-AESL-call scale) — this is what makes an
  end-to-end, honestly-verified key recovery browser-runnable. It is not the
  full algebraic attack: recovering a full random 256-bit key is 2^130 data /
  2^209 time (ePrint 2025/1203) and is annotated, never executed. The paper's
  AESL differential machinery (Theorem 1 enumeration, the MITM key equation)
  is implemented, unit-tested, and now runnable in-browser one step at a time —
  but the reduced keyspace, not that machinery, is what the end-to-end key
  recovery drives.
- **The distinct, stronger result:** [Bille & Tischhauser, ePrint 2025/1180](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1180), ToSC 2026, revised 16 June 2026, report full key recovery with 2^128 data and at most 2^129 time in a nonce-respecting setting with decryption queries. They also give a query/success trade-off with total cost divided by success probability at most 2^129. This is not Hu’s 2^209-time / 2^130-data result. Both full-size costs remain infeasible; the reduced-seed browser search reproduces neither. The visible comparison keeps source version, success and oracle access separate.
```

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- Nonce/IV reuse in AES-256-GCM breaks both confidentiality and authentication, so each message needs a fresh, unique nonce.
- Encrypting to an unauthenticated public key invites a man-in-the-middle who substitutes their own key — the recipient's key must be bound to a verified identity. The ECIES tab lets you mount this attack for real and then watch a signature check defeat it.
- Public-key encryption alone provides no sender authentication; anyone can encrypt to a recipient, so a separate signature is needed to prove origin.
- ECIES and RSA-OAEP depend on matching curve/KDF/AEAD and padding parameters between sender and recipient — a mismatch causes decryption failure or weakened security.
- Private keys generated and held in the browser are only as safe as the device and session; this demo is not a key-management system.
- A protected SUCI does not conceal the home-network identifier or routing indicator; null-scheme output copies the identifier bytes unchanged. Identity concealment alone does not prevent every tracking technique or authenticate a base station. The example's generated home-network keys are local teaching keys, never a real operator's provisioning.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 9798 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

Iron Letter is a browser-based demo of ECIES P-256 and RSA-OAEP hybrid encryption built on the Web Crypto API. ECIES P-256 combines ECDH, HKDF-SHA256, and AES-256-GCM, while RSA-2048 and RSA-4096 use RSA-OAEP to wrap an AES-256-GCM content key. The problem it solves is public-key message sealing, where anyone can encrypt to a recipient but only the matching private key can decrypt. This is an asymmetric security model, with symmetric AES used inside each hybrid envelope for message confidentiality and integrity.

The separate **5G identity** tab applies the same broad public-key idea to a different and specifically defined job: concealing the subscriber digits of an IMSI-based permanent subscriber identifier before 5G authentication. It runs ECIES **Profile A** with fresh X25519, ANSI X9.63 KDF/SHA-256, AES-128-CTR, and an eight-byte HMAC-SHA-256 tag. These are not the P-256/HKDF/AES-GCM parameters of Iron Letter's message-sealing workbench. The field display distinguishes protected MSIN from clear home-network and routing information, then compares Profile A with the null scheme and an emergency Identity Response. It models the identity-concealment step, not a complete 5G NAS encoder or a conformant mobile-network implementation.

It is built as a scaffolded two-party workbench: keygen mints distinct keypairs for **Alice** (sender), **Bob** (recipient), and **Eve** (an eavesdropper). Alice always seals to *Bob's* public key — never her own — so the directional meaning of asymmetry is unavoidable, and a one-click "open with Eve's wrong key" button lets you watch a real AES-GCM authentication failure. For ECIES it renders an **ECDH convergence panel** that shows both sides — `ephemeral private × Bob public` and `Bob private × ephemeral public` — computing the *identical* 32-byte shared secret (all real WebCrypto derivations), which then flows through HKDF into the AES key. Beyond that passive failure, the ECIES tab lets you **mount an active man-in-the-middle**: Eve substitutes her own ECDH public key on the wire, Alice seals to it, and the panel prints the two secrets side by side — Alice's `ephemeral private × the key she was handed` against Bob's `Bob private × ephemeral public` — byte-compared and *different*, while Eve's real AES-GCM decrypt recovers Alice's plaintext and (optionally) re-seals her own words to Bob's genuine key, which Bob opens with every check passing. Re-running the identical attack against a channel where Bob's key arrives signed by his long-term ECDSA identity key aborts it: the verification returns false, Alice never seals, and a control verification over Bob's genuine key returns true in the same run to prove the check is not simply rejecting everything. Ciphertext is mapped onto a color-coded **byte-layout strip** (ephemeral key ‖ IV ‖ ciphertext+tag for ECIES; wrapped AES key ‖ IV ‖ ciphertext for RSA), and jargon (ECDH, HKDF, OAEP, SPKI/PKCS8, ephemeral, base64url, symmetric-equivalent bits) carries inline glossary tooltips. Teaching clarity is layered on top of the real cryptography; no primitive is weakened and every round-trip is KAT-backed.
```

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- Passphrase reuse across multiple containers can break deniability, because deterministic key/nonce/offset derivation enables cross-container analysis and two-time-pad style leakage.
- Guessing a passphrase exposes its own message, configured role and offset. It does not automatically yield the other independently chosen passphrase, key or plaintext. Knowing one slot and the nonoverlap rule can restrict possible positions for the other slot without decrypting it. Correlated passwords can make the second password easier to guess; reuse across containers adds the separate deterministic-key/nonce risks documented in the threat model.
- JavaScript string handling is an implementation pitfall, because passphrases enter the app as immutable JS strings that cannot be securely zeroized like WASM buffers.
- Unicode normalization mismatches can lock users out, because visually identical passphrases may encode to different UTF-8 byte sequences on different platforms.
- A non-plausible decoy undermines coercion resistance, because deniable encryption relies on the revealed message being believable to an adversary.
```

```markdown
## What It Is

Shadow Vault is a browser demonstration of deniable encryption that combines Argon2id key derivation, ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD encryption, and SHA-256 domain separation in a fixed-size random container. It demonstrates two independently encrypted slots in the same blob. A format-aware reader knows two slots are written and can classify a disclosed passphrase as the configured real or decoy role by authenticating the public role/counter candidates. This requires no knowledge of the other passphrase, but does not recover the unopened plaintext or establish the meaning or importance of either message. It provides no role privacy; hiding labels in the UI does not change this. The cryptographic core is symmetric encryption with password-based key derivation, executed in Rust/WASM through a Web Worker. It is not asymmetric, threshold, or zero-knowledge cryptography, and it is not positioned as production deniable storage.
```

**Stated limitations (page)**:

- _(honesty, index.html)_ Cryptographic honesty: the modular-arithmetic checks and Web Crypto primitives in Exhibits 02, 03, 04, 05, 07 and 08 are real. Exhibit 07 runs exact BigInt arithmetic over a published 2048-bit group and a fresh WebCrypto RSA modulus; Exhibit 08 runs the sum-check interactive proof and a bounded GKR layer walk in exact prime-field arithmetic, and is neither zero-knowledge nor a SNARK; Exhibits 01 and 06 are clearly-labelled conceptual models.
- _(honesty, exhibits/cave.html)_ Cryptographic honesty: this exhibit is a conceptual thought experiment to teach the shape of zero-knowledge proofs. It does not claim production-grade cryptographic parameters.
- _(honesty, exhibits/commit-reveal.html)_ Cryptographic honesty: SHA-256 is computed by the browser Web Crypto API. This scenario uses educational-scale values for clarity and speed, not a complete production auction protocol.
- _(honesty, exhibits/fiat-shamir.html)_ Cryptographic honesty: challenge generation is real SHA-256 over transcript inputs and verification is real modular arithmetic. Parameters are intentionally small for readability.
- _(honesty, exhibits/graph-coloring.html)_ Cryptographic honesty: each region is committed with a real SHA-256(color ‖ nonce) digest, and on reveal the opening is re-hashed and checked against the published commitment. The challenge-reveal logic and soundness amplification ((5/6)k) of ZK graph coloring are preserved faithfully. The zero-knowledge property is exhibited rather than asserted: the extractor bench at the bottom of this page runs two real attacks — a bounded SHA-256 preimage search against the published digests, and a full enumeration of the colourings the transcript leaves possible — and prints only what they returned. The graph and colour palette are small for a legible walkthrough, not for deployment security.
- _(honesty, exhibits/scenario-presets.html)_ Preset contract: each URL captures seed + behavior mode + optional auto-run. Same URL means same flow, making debugging and demos repeatable.
- _(honesty, exhibits/schnorr.html)_ Cryptographic honesty: the verification equation and modular arithmetic are real. Parameters are deliberately tiny for human-readable walkthroughs and animation speed, not for deployment security.
- _(honesty, exhibits/sigma-family.html)_ Cryptographic honesty: Okamoto and GQ use exact BigInt equations at 2048 bits, with SHA-256 deriving h from the seed shown below. The p = 47 witness-independence census is explicitly a complete toy model. This is inspectable teaching code, not a constant-time production library.
- _(honesty, exhibits/snark.html)_ Cryptographic honesty: this exhibit teaches the architecture of zk-SNARK systems (setup/proving/verification and public/private split). It is intentionally not a real SNARK implementation or security parameterization. Two pieces are genuinely computed and re-checked by the verifier rather than asserted: the arithmetic relation y = w² + 3w + 7, and a real SHA-256 digest binding the public input to the proof envelope — which is why the tamper preset is rejected on the numbers. Everything else here — trusted setup, proving key, succinctness — is narrated, not performed.
- _(honesty, exhibits/sumcheck-gkr.html)_ Cryptographic honesty: every value below comes from exact BigInt modular arithmetic in the prime field you select. The verifier checks a degree bound and a recurrence in every round and draws each challenge only after that round's message is fixed. The tiny-field census is a complete enumeration for teaching, not a security parameter. This is inspectable teaching code for an interactive proof: it is not zero-knowledge, not a SNARK, and not a constant-time library.
- _(honesty, exhibits/transcript-lab.html)_ How to use, and what is real: load the latest transcript from an exhibit or paste JSON manually, then compare transcript semantics and verifier outcomes side by side. For Fiat-Shamir transcripts this page does not take the recorded challenge on trust — it re-derives it with a real SHA-256 digest over the transcript's own (R, y, message) and reports match or mismatch. The remaining rows are field-level comparison of the JSON, not verification: this is a teaching inspector for proof traces, not a proof checker.

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- Reusing Schnorr nonces (`r`) can leak the secret (`x`) from two transcripts, which breaks the core secrecy guarantee of identification proofs.
- Using small or weak group parameters makes discrete-log attacks practical, so a verifier equation that passes in the toy demo would not imply real-world security.
- Omitting transcript/domain separation details in Fiat-Shamir challenge derivation can enable replay or malleability across contexts, undermining non-interactive soundness assumptions.
- The Fiat-Shamir exhibit deliberately reduces its SHA-256 digest to a challenge in `1..50`. With `?seed=3`, the original and altered messages have different full digests but the same challenge `26`, and verification passes. This is a toy challenge-domain collision, not a SHA-256 collision. All verdict text follows the actual equation and shows original/altered challenges; an unavailable hash produces no tamper verdict. Copy/Replay preserve the original proof. See [RFC 8235 §2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8235.html#section-2.3) for production-sized challenge and context requirements; this small-parameter exhibit is not an RFC-conforming implementation.
- Reusing or biasing commit-reveal nonces weakens hiding and can leak bid information before reveal, defeating fairness of the commit phase.
- Failing to enforce reveal windows in commit-reveal protocols allows strategic non-reveal (griefing), which is a protocol-level failure even when hash checks are correct.
- Reusing an Okamoto or GQ commitment across two different challenges exposes the representation or RSA root; the rewind panels compute that extraction rather than merely warning about it.
- Choosing a tiny GQ exponent also creates a tiny challenge space. The deliberately broken e = 3 mode shows a prover with only public y passing about one time in three; e = 65537 is the default.
- A sum-check verifier that drops the per-round degree bound can be beaten by a full-field interpolant of degree at most p − 1 that agrees with the honest message everywhere but one point. The exhibit prints its actual degree and shows it rejected on degree only when that degree exceeds the statement's public X1 bound; when the public bound already permits it, the page labels the example as not a degree-bound violation and reports its actual acceptance count. The mutation suite kills a verifier that stops enforcing a genuinely exceeded bound.
- A sum-check verifier's challenges must be drawn after the round's message is fixed. The exhibit's deterministic teaching seed exists so runs replay, and the page labels it as not cryptographically secure verifier randomness: a prover who knows the seed knows every challenge in advance.
- Static transcript replay rechecks structure and arithmetic but carries no timestamps, so it cannot prove that a recorded challenge was historically sampled after its message or was unpredictable. Those properties come from the live phase guard and fresh-random mode, respectively.
- Fields of 13, 7 or 5 elements make the soundness arithmetic readable, not meaningful. The census counts the constructed lie polynomial's actual roots rather than assuming every degree is attained, and the page caps probability bounds at 1 and marks raw union sums at least 1 as vacuous.
- The wrong-output and altered-line controls are probabilistic soundness examples, not guaranteed rejection scripts: a wrong output can survive at a root of its difference polynomial, and q(t) + t(t − 1) is unchanged when the verifier's line challenge is 0 or 1.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 16608 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

ZK Proof Lab is an interactive educational demo for zero-knowledge proof workflows. Six of the eight exhibits use cryptographically real primitives in the browser: the `Graph 3-Coloring ZKP` commits every region with real Web Crypto SHA-256; `Schnorr Identification`, `Fiat-Shamir`, and `Beyond Schnorr` run exact modular arithmetic; `Hash Commit-Reveal` uses real SHA-256 commitments; and `Sum-Check and GKR` executes the sum-check interactive proof and a bounded GKR layer walk in exact prime-field arithmetic. `Beyond Schnorr` adds Okamoto representation proofs in the RFC 3526 2048-bit group and GQ RSA-root proofs over fresh 2048-bit WebCrypto moduli, alongside a clearly labelled p = 47 exhaustive model. `Sum-Check and GKR` is an interactive-proof and verifiable-computation lesson, not a zero-knowledge one: it says so on the page, and it is not a SNARK. The remaining two exhibits (`Ali Baba Cave`, `zk-SNARK intuition`) are clearly-labelled conceptual models. The lab addresses proving knowledge or correctness without disclosing the secret witness. It is teaching code, not an audited or constant-time cryptographic library.

The zero-knowledge property itself is exhibited rather than asserted. The Graph 3-Coloring page carries an **extractor bench** that lets you attack the hiding claim and watch what the attack actually returns. Attack 1 is a bounded brute-force preimage search that hashes ~200,000 candidate `(colour, nonce)` openings with real Web Crypto SHA-256 against the digests the page just published; it recovers nothing, and reports the fraction of the keyspace that budget covered (~2e-34) alongside the average cost of a real break (~5e38 hashes), so the failure reads as a measurement of scale rather than a claim. The identical attacker function is then re-run against the same colours committed under a deliberately weakened 8-bit nonce, where it recovers every opening in 768 hashes — the only variable is the nonce space. Attack 2 is the extractor a verifier could run offline: given only the challenged edges and the opened colour pairs, it enumerates all 3^5 = 243 colourings and keeps every one no round rules out. Because the palette is re-permuted each round, the candidate set converges on the 18 proper colourings of this graph — which is exactly the statement being proved — and never on a single one, while folding in the broken commitments from Attack 1 collapses it to 6.

There are no published known-answer vectors for the interactive Okamoto or GQ protocols. Their tests instead pin the exact RFC 3526 group-14 prime, independently establish that p and q = (p − 1)/2 are prime, recompute the deterministic h derivation, and verify every protocol and extraction equation with independent arithmetic.
```

**Description**: Run a real (if small) STARK in your browser — build a trace polynomial and AIR constraints, commit with a SHA-256 Merkle tree, and inspect every check that accepts the honest proof and rejects the supplied tampered fixture.  — _read from index.html_

**Why it matters**: STARKs need no trusted setup. Their commitments are hash based, while FRI contributes information-theoretic proximity errors and the non-interactive Fiat-Shamir/BCS step is analyzed in a random-oracle model. Their post-quantum security is therefore conjectured  — _read from index.html_

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Large proofs** — STARK proofs run ~45–200 KB versus 128 bytes for Groth16, a real cost wherever bandwidth or storage is tight.
- **Expensive on-chain verification** — STARK verification is far costlier than Groth16 (~50 ms vs ~1 ms), so tight gas budgets can make it impractical.
- **Query arithmetic is not protocol soundness** — at rate `ρ=1/8` and eight queries, `−log₂(ρ⁸)=24` is exact arithmetic for a capacity-level sampling model. It is displayed as a **heuristic query term**, never as FRI or STARK security. The unique-decoding-radius query-only reference is about 6.64 bits only when both the actual distance and `θ` reach `(1−ρ)/2`. If the actual distance is at least the Johnson radius and `θ` approaches `1−√ρ` from below, the query-only value approaches 12 bits as a strict limit. Neither includes fold-round MCA errors or surrounding protocol terms.
- **The complete bounds are not established here** — applying CL146 requires the actual initial-word distance `δ`, a tradeoff `θ`, and every fold's MCA error. An end-to-end non-interactive STARK analysis must additionally justify AIR/composition algebraic errors, Merkle/hash binding and Fiat-Shamir/BCS loss. The executable ledger leaves both results `NOT ESTABLISHED` rather than treating missing terms as zero.
- **Field choice matters** — FRI needs a field with high 2-adicity (here `3·2³⁰+1`); a field like `2³¹−1` with 2-adicity 1 cannot support honest power-of-two evaluation domains or real folding.
- **Toy simplifications** — short traces and Lagrange interpolation (instead of NTT) keep the demo legible but are not how a production STARK scales; the ZK property here is shown empirically, not via a full simulator proof.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 12433 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

STARK Tower is an **honest, working** browser demonstration of zk-STARKs (Scalable Transparent ARguments of Knowledge; Ben-Sasson et al., 2018) — the post-quantum alternative to pairing-based SNARKs. STARKs require no trusted setup and scale quasi-linearly. Their commitments rely on hash security, FRI contributes information-theoretic proximity errors, and the non-interactive Fiat-Shamir/BCS step is analyzed in a random-oracle model; their post-quantum security is therefore conjectured, not proved. They express computation as an Arithmetic Intermediate Representation (AIR) of polynomial constraints and use FRI (Fast Reed–Solomon IOP) as a transparent low-degree test. The cost is larger proofs (~45–200 KB vs 128 bytes for Groth16).

What makes this demo different from a hand-wave: **the verifier rejects the supplied tampered fixtures without re-running the computation.** It checks authenticated openings, composition consistency, membership in the final degree-`<1` code and sampled FRI fold relations. Tampering one trace cell makes the generated constraint quotient fail polynomial division; for the transcript-derived challenges in this run, its eight final evaluations do not agree and verification rejects. A dedicated **quotient exhibit** makes that causal path visible with exact field arithmetic. This is empirical evidence for the generated fixtures, not a universal soundness experiment.
```

**Name (H1)**: SNARK Arena  — _read from index.html_

**Subtitle**: zk-SNARKs · Groth16 & PLONK  — _read from index.html_

**Description**: Drive R1CS circuits and witnesses through both proving systems, run a real in-browser trusted-setup ceremony, and watch a leaked toxic-waste τ forge a proof.  — _read from index.html_

**Why it matters**: SNARKs secure Zcash, zkEVM rollups, and private identity — billions of dollars of value ride on soundness. If a ceremony's secret τ is ever leaked, anyone can mint proofs of false statements and the whole system silently breaks.  — _read from index.html_

**Card copy**: Generate and verify real BN254 Groth16 proofs, then compare a deliberately weak XOR relation with an in-circuit bit-constrained repair that rejects the same non-binary assignment. Separate toy-field panels demonstrate powers of tau and an accepted KZG opening forged with retained toxic waste; PLONK remains comparison-only.

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Private input is not necessarily confidential.** The live proof panel publishes `out = x³ + x + 5`. All 21 slider values 0–20 have distinct outputs below field wraparound, so `out=35` identifies `x=3` without inspecting the proof. The toy playground likewise has only `x=3` in its 0–9 slider range, while its full field still has the documented three roots. This example teaches proof mechanics, not witness confidentiality; zero knowledge cannot undo information already implied by public inputs. This is separate from the unverified setup provenance described below.

- **Trusted-setup toxic waste** — anyone who retains the secret `τ` from the setup ceremony can forge proofs for false statements; the powers-of-tau and KZG-forgery exhibits demonstrate exactly this.
- **Single-party setup** — trust rests entirely on that participant's honest generation and secret destruction. Multi-party setup distributes that trust: at least one honest participant must destroy their contribution. Participant count alone does not prove destruction or soundness.
- **Not post-quantum** — Groth16 and PLONK rest on pairing-based assumptions and fall to a quantum adversary; use STARKs where long-term quantum resistance is required.
- **Under-constrained relations** — proof validity establishes only the relation actually encoded. The constraint-gap case study makes this concrete: a weak relation accepts a genuine, unmodified Groth16 proof for public inputs `(2,2)` and output `−4 mod r`, even though the intended Boolean-XOR computation rejects non-bits. The repair is `a(a−1)=0` and `b(b−1)=0` inside the circuit, followed by circuit-specific artifact regeneration; a browser input check is not a proof-relation repair.
- **Toy-field intuition** — the interactive panels use small fields so values verify by hand, and there is more than one: the R1CS circuit playground runs over `F₈₁₉₁` (2¹³ − 1), while the powers-of-tau ceremony and KZG-forgery exhibits use `F₁₇`. Both are toy and both are labeled in-app; real deployments need 254-bit curves, and the demo's proof-size/timing figures in Exhibits 02–04 are labeled illustrative.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 15766 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

SNARK Arena demonstrates the two most deployed zk-SNARK proving systems: Groth16 (Groth, EUROCRYPT 2016) and PLONK (Gabizon et al., 2019). Both are succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge: under their security assumptions, they prove knowledge of a witness satisfying a circuit without disclosing additional information beyond the public statement, in small proofs. That statement can itself reveal the witness. Groth16 produces 128-byte proofs on BN254 with per-circuit trusted setup — that is the compressed encoding; the same three group elements are 256 bytes uncompressed, which is what snarkjs writes and what the live-proof panel reports. PLONK produces approximately 400-byte proofs with a universal trusted setup reusable across circuits. Both rely on pairing-based assumptions and are not post-quantum secure.
```

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Performance overhead:** FHE ciphertexts are large and bootstrapping is slow, so throughput and latency are far worse than plaintext computation.
- **Limited operations:** practical FHE supports a constrained set of operations and bit-widths (here, addition over `FheUint8`); arbitrary programs are expensive or infeasible.
- **No result integrity:** homomorphic evaluation hides inputs but does not by itself prove the server computed the right function — a malicious server could return a wrong-but-valid ciphertext.
- **Malicious-server feedback oracle:** a server can alter returned ciphertexts and learn from a client that reports decryption errors. Chaturvedi et al. demonstrated full key recovery against TFHE/FHEW under repeated client feedback, which does not demonstrate a break of this demo. Blind Oracle compares the result in the browser and sends neither the plaintext nor its match/mismatch verdict back to the server. This closes that feedback path in the demonstrated flow, but does not establish side-channel resistance on the client. See the [original attack (ePrint 2022/1563)](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1563) and the [2025 survey (ePrint 2025/867)](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/867).
- **Metadata still leaks:** request timing, ciphertext sizes, and access patterns remain visible to the server even though plaintext does not.
- **Client-side key management:** security depends entirely on the client key never leaking — lose it and the data is unrecoverable, expose it and confidentiality is gone.
- **The Oracle is a free-tier service and can be unavailable.** The demo handles that explicitly (degraded mode) rather than pretending otherwise, but the headline add genuinely does require it.
- **The local bench is a teaching model, not secure encryption.** Its 48-bit DGHV-inspired modulus is trivially breakable. The unsigned no-wrap interval applies to this local model, not to TFHE's parameters or security.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 17468 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

Blind Oracle is a browser-to-server demonstration of **Fully Homomorphic Encryption** using [TFHE-rs](https://github.com/zama-ai/tfhe-rs) and programmable bootstrapping (PBS) over encrypted `FheUint8` values. An `FheUint8` is radix-decomposed into shortint blocks and each block operation runs a PBS; _gate_ bootstrapping is the term for TFHE's boolean API, which this demo does not use. The client encrypts two inputs, the server performs homomorphic addition, and the client decrypts the encrypted result locally. This solves the problem of outsourcing computation while keeping plaintext hidden from the compute provider. The security model is asymmetric homomorphic encryption (public evaluation key on the server, secret decryption key kept client-side), with post-quantum lattice-based foundations through TFHE.

### Why one step runs off-device

Every crypto-lab demo is browser-only, and this one is the exception in exactly one place: the homomorphic **add** runs on a small remote service. That is not a shortcut. Zama's browser (WASM) build of TFHE-rs exposes key generation, encryption, decryption and serialization — and no evaluation operations at all: there is no `add`, `mul` or any other homomorphic method on `FheUint8` in the bundled `tfhe.d.ts`, and `set_server_key` has nothing to apply. The evaluation therefore has to happen where the TFHE-rs evaluation API exists. That split is also, conveniently, the real FHE deployment shape: a client that holds the secret key, and a compute provider that holds only an evaluation key.

Two things follow, and the demo now does both:

- **A remote dependency must degrade, not dead-end.** If the Oracle is asleep, redeployed, or gone for good, the page offers _Continue without the Oracle_ and keeps everything local working — key generation, encryption, the ciphertext inspector, and the local multiply bench — with a banner naming exactly which one step is unavailable.
- **A multiplication that is only described is not demonstrated.** The **local multiply bench** performs real homomorphic multiplications in the tab, on a second (deliberately tiny) scheme, and lets you keep going until the noise budget runs out.

### The local multiply bench

`src/toyFhe.ts` implements a DGHV-inspired (van Dijk–Gentry–Halevi–Vaikuntanathan, 2010) unsigned, base-256 teaching model: `Enc(m) = m + 256r + qp`, `Dec(c) = (c mod p) mod 256`. Addition adds the tracked noise term; multiplication multiplies it. The decoder reduces into `[0,p)`, so the exact first no-wrap interval is `0 ≤ noise < p`, including the entire interval between `p/2` and `p`. The table displays bit lengths, while the verdict checks exact integers; equal bit lengths alone do not establish whether noise is below `p`. With the default parameters, hundreds of additions stay inside this interval while the **third** multiplication crosses it. Each step reports actual decryption against the expected plaintext byte.

**Toy scale, stated on the page and here:** the original paper's security analysis does not apply to this tiny 48-bit adaptation. This is not secure encryption and must never be used as such. [DGHV 2010, §2](https://www.uvm.edu/~cvincen1/files/teaching/pcmi/DGHV2010.pdf) defines centered residues in `(-p/2,p/2]`; its `p/2` bound belongs to that decoder, not this unsigned byte model. At `noise = p` the first wrap changes the decoded byte. Beyond the no-wrap interval, particular wrap counts can preserve the byte (for example, 256 wraps because `p` is odd), but an observed match does not restore a general correctness guarantee. The bench demonstrates local noise growth and wrapping; it does not reproduce TFHE's parameters or implement programmable bootstrapping.

Verification includes fixed-key controls at `floor(p/2)`, `p-1`, `p`, `p+1`, negative noise and a matching byte after 256 wraps. A production-browser control runs the actual bench with scoped toy randomness after real TFHE key generation: 128 additions and two multiplica

```

**Stated limitations (page)**:

- _(disclaimer, src/main.ts)_ ⚠ This is an educational toy implementation with n=8. 128-bit security is set by the (n, log q) pair — the HE Standard permits n=4096 only up to log q ≤ 109 — so production CKKS uses n ≥ 8192 to afford a real modulus chain. Do not use this code for any real cryptographic purpose.

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- CKKS is *approximate*: every ciphertext carries noise, so results are never exact. Using it where an exact answer is required (financial totals, equality checks, cryptographic values) silently yields wrong results.
- Each homomorphic multiplication consumes a level in the modulus chain; running out of levels without bootstrapping corrupts the result, so the multiplicative depth must be planned in advance.
- Scale and rescaling management is error-prone: forgetting to rescale, or combining ciphertexts at mismatched scales, produces meaningless plaintext on decryption.
- Parameter choice (ring degree, modulus chain, scale) sets both the security level and the available compute budget — too small a ring or too large a modulus can break the underlying RLWE security.
- Approximate-decryption leakage (the IND-CPA^D class of attacks): handing raw decrypted CKKS results to an untrusted party can leak information about the secret key unless the decryption output is noise-flooded.

- **Validity-response leakage:** [Bian et al., ePrint 2026/2490 (15 October 2026)](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2490) report key recovery in CKKS deployments combining public coefficient-to-slot (C2S) evaluation keys with an observable client one-bit validity response. Their attack is conditional on this deployment surface and does not break RLWE or CKKS IND-CPA security. Keeping raw decrypted values private alone does not address this separate feedback channel; protocols must assess what client reactions reveal to an untrusted evaluator. This symmetric toy engine has no public encryption key or C2S evaluation layer and does not reproduce the attack. Noise flooding for approximate-decryption leakage is not established here as a remedy for this reaction attack.

  The deployment caveat now includes a **conceptual feedback interaction**: select a hidden ternary coefficient, make the public-key and C2S capabilities available or unavailable, choose whether the client's validity bit is visible, and try abstract support/positive-sign probes. With all preconditions present, each modeled response filters the attacker's candidate set; keeping it private removes that particular observation. The decisions reflect the paper's two-phase support/sign logic, but the panel constructs no CKKS query, proves no noise bound, and makes no key-recovery or security claim about this toy engine. The learner-only audit is separate from the attacker view.
```

**README, first section** (full text in `labs.jsonl`, field `readme`; 11943 bytes):

```markdown
## What It Is

CKKS Lab demonstrates CKKS (Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song, ASIACRYPT 2017) — the Fully Homomorphic Encryption scheme for approximate arithmetic on real numbers. Unlike BGV/BFV which produce exact integer results, CKKS deliberately introduces small approximation errors to enable efficient floating-point arithmetic on encrypted data. A CKKS ciphertext encodes a vector of real numbers (n/2 slots for polynomial degree n) and supports vectorized addition and multiplication directly on ciphertexts. CKKS is the FHE scheme behind encrypted machine learning inference — the ability to evaluate a neural network on encrypted input without the server ever seeing the plaintext data.

The demo is built for a newcomer to follow start-to-finish: it opens with a one-click "encrypt 3.14, get 3.1401 back" round-trip, then makes the scheme's hardest idea — the canonical embedding — watchable by showing 4 real slot values flow into 8 integer polynomial coefficients and then pick up the tiny RLWE noise term. Ciphertexts render as legible centered "signal + noise" coefficients (with a raw-hex toggle), and you can corrupt a single coefficient and watch a decrypted slot drift, proving the encryption is real by interaction rather than by prose. Advanced material (the FHE decision panel, the RLWE foundation, scheme comparisons) is tucked behind "go deeper" reveals so it never blocks the first hands-on success.
```

**Description**: Encrypt integers, add and multiply them on a blind server, then decrypt via Δ·m + e and watch the noise budget shrink until decryption fails.  — _read from src/main.ts_

**Why it matters**: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on data it can never read — the promise behind private cloud, medical, and financial analytics. The noise budget is what makes or breaks it: overflow it and the answer is silently lost.  — _read from src/main.ts_

**Card copy**: Explore toy BFV integer homomorphic encryption with addition, multiplication, a noise-budget visualizer, relinearization, and polynomial-coefficient packing. BGV and production SIMD batching are discussed, not implemented.

**README — What Can Go Wrong**:

```text
- **Decryption-feedback research — 20 October 2026.** Ordinary encryption security (IND-CPA), correct decryption, and security when an adversary learns computation results (IND-CPA-D) are different guarantees. Choe, Kang and Stehlé report attacks on particular BFV/BGV configurations using heuristic correctness assumptions, with experiments in OpenFHE and HElib. Crafted operations can exceed heuristic noise bounds; two attacks recover keys, while a third breaks indistinguishability. Parameter tables and noise estimates alone do not establish security in this feedback model. This browser lab does not reproduce those attacks or establish that its implementation is vulnerable. [Choe, Kang and Stehlé, *New IND-CPA-D Attacks on BFV and BGV*, ePrint 2026/2546](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2546), received 19 October and revised 20 October 2026; accepted to ACM CCS 2026. **Demonstrated results; attack-model-conditional.**

- **Noise budget exhaustion.** Every homomorphic operation grows ciphertext noise; exceed the budget and decryption silently returns garbage. Multiplicative depth must be planned before the circuit is built.
- **Wrong scheme for the data.** BGV/BFV are integer schemes. Forcing real-valued or approximate workloads onto them gives poor results — CKKS exists for that, with its own approximation caveats.
- **Insecure parameter selection.** Polynomial degree and modulus must follow the Homomorphic Encryption Standard; ad-hoc parameters can drop below the claimed security level or fail to support the intended depth.
- **No integrity by default.** FHE ciphertexts are malleable by design (that is the whole point), so a malicious server can tamper with results unless you add separate verification. IND-CPA security does not imply CCA security.
- **Bootstrapping cost and timing.** Bootstrapping refreshes noise but is expensive and must run before overflow, not after; treating it as free or as a recovery step after corruption does not work.
```
